opus-5.5.text:
I'd say the motivation came from a different place, and honestly it came earlier. My background is in 3D vision. During my PhD and postdoc I worked on understanding objects in three dimensions: their pose, their parts, how they articulate. Over time I kept running into the same wall. You can build a vision system that recognizes a mug very well, but recognition isn't understanding. Real understanding means knowing how to grasp it, how to pour from it, how it behaves when you push it. That only comes from interacting with the physical world. So for me, embodiment was the natural next step of the vision research itself, not a reaction to a hot topic.

When ChatGPT came out, and then work like PaLM-E, a lot of people got excited because suddenly there seemed to be a "brain" that could reason, plan, and talk, and the obvious question was: can we put this brain into a robot? That excitement is valuable. It brought attention, talent, and funding into the field. But I think it also created a misconception that the language model is the hard part and the body is just an interface. In my view it's almost the opposite. High-level planning in language is relatively tractable now. The real bottleneck is the low-level skill: dexterous grasping, manipulation, robust control in messy, unstructured environments. Large models don't solve that for you, because there's no internet-scale dataset of robot actions the way there's internet-scale text.

So when we set up the center, the core question wasn't "how do we connect an LLM to a robot." It was "how do we get generalizable physical skills, and where does the data come from?" That's why we've put so much emphasis on simulation and synthetic data. We use physically realistic simulation to generate huge amounts of grasping and manipulation data, then work hard on sim-to-real transfer, and combine that with a smaller amount of real-world data. That path is less glamorous than a demo of a robot chatting with you, but I believe it's what actually scales.

To put it simply: the post-ChatGPT wave asked what a smart brain can do with a body. We started from what a body needs to learn in order to be truly useful, and how to give it enough experience to learn that. The two meet in the middle eventually, but the starting points are quite different.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the motivation came earlier and that embodiment was a continuation of vision research, “not a reaction to a hot topic.”

r002.rationale: The candidate argues for learning useful physical skills, but does not say embodied intelligence merits research even if it does not lead to general intelligence.

r003.rationale: The candidate says ChatGPT and PaLM-E brought attention, talent, and funding to the field, but does not identify Chinese investors seeking out embodied AI researchers.

fable-5.1.text:
Actually, it's a question of timing. The Embodied Intelligence Center at Peking University was set up in 2021, and the Galaxy General Robot project started in early 2023, right around when ChatGPT and PaLM-E came out. So people naturally assume we were riding that wave. But the thinking behind it goes back much earlier.

My background is in 3D vision. I did my PhD at Stanford with Leonidas Guibas, and most of that work was about understanding objects and scenes in three dimensions: point clouds, pose estimation, articulated objects, things like that. Toward the end of my PhD, a question kept bothering me. We were getting very good at perceiving the world, but perception that doesn't lead to action is kind of a dead end. You can label every object in a room perfectly, and nothing happens. The real test of whether a machine understands the physical world is whether it can do something with that understanding. So I started pushing toward manipulation, grasping, interacting with articulated objects, and that led very naturally to robotics.

When I came back to PKU, I wanted to build a group around exactly that bridge, from 3D perception to physical interaction. At the time, embodied AI was not a popular phrase in China at all. Most people thought of it as a niche corner of computer vision or a subfield of robotics, not as a frontier of AI. There was no hype to attach to. Frankly, it was harder to recruit students then, because the obvious exciting thing was large language models.

So the difference, I think, comes down to this. The post-ChatGPT enthusiasm was mostly a top-down bet: large models are powerful, so let's point them at robots and see what happens. Our starting point was bottom-up. We had spent years on the concrete problems, generalizable grasping, understanding how objects move and deform, getting policies to transfer from simulation to the real world, and we had a fairly sober view of how hard the physical side really is. Language models don't solve the fact that your data is scarce, that the world is 3D and continuous, that a gripper slips.

That said, I don't want to sound dismissive of the wave. PaLM-E and the later work showed that foundation models can genuinely contribute to high-level reasoning and task decomposition for robots, and that changed what we could aim for. What it did for us was to confirm the direction and raise the ceiling, not to create the direction. The way I'd put it is that we were already walking down the road, and then suddenly a lot of people started running alongside us. That's good for the field. It just means you have to be a bit careful not to confuse the noise for the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says the Center was established in 2021, before ChatGPT, and that the later wave confirmed the direction rather than creating it.

r002.rationale: The response argues for physical interaction and robotics, but does not say embodied intelligence merits research independently of whether it leads to general intelligence.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Chinese investors seeking out people working on embodied AI after PaLM-E’s release.

astra-6.text:
I would separate the underlying motivation from the excitement around a particular wave of models. For me, the central question is how intelligence can act in the physical world: how a robot connects perception with action, learns from interaction, and handles situations it hasn’t encountered before. That is a reason to build a sustained research effort, regardless of which model is attracting attention.

ChatGPT and PaLM-E brought much more attention to those questions and opened up possibilities. But excitement alone doesn’t resolve the difficulty of getting a physical system to work reliably. A robot has to act under uncertainty, and its mistakes have physical consequences.

So I would describe the motivation for the center as building the capability to work on those underlying problems over time. The new wave of models can help us pursue that goal, but it shouldn’t define the goal itself.

r001.rationale: It says the center’s motivation is to address underlying physical-world intelligence problems, independent of attention to ChatGPT or any particular model wave.

r002.rationale: It supports sustained research on embodied intelligence, but does not say that this research merits pursuit even if it does not lead to general intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Chinese investors or say PaLM-E’s release prompted them to seek out embodied-AI researchers.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the motivation was a longer-term research question: how can intelligence move beyond processing information to perceiving and acting in the physical world? Establishing an Embodied Intelligence Center was a way to bring those pieces together—perception, learning, decision-making, and control—and study them as one problem.

ChatGPT and PaLM-E brought much more attention to that direction, and they gave us reasons to be excited about what large models could contribute. But I would distinguish that excitement from the underlying motivation. A model can describe an action very convincingly; getting a robot to carry it out reliably, adapt to an unfamiliar environment, and learn from what happens is another challenge. That is the challenge I wanted the center to focus on.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the Center grew from a longer-term research question and distinguishes that underlying motivation from the excitement ChatGPT brought.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say embodied intelligence merits research independently of whether it leads to general intelligence.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not mention Chinese investors or PaLM-E’s release prompting them to seek out embodied AI researchers.
